prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My desk is cleared of the litter of ages; Before me glitter the fair white pages; My fountain pen is clean and filled, And the noise of the office has long been stilled. Roget’s Thesaurus is at my hand, And I’m ready to do some work that’s grand, Dignified, eminent, great, momentous, Memorable, worthy of note, portentous, Beautiful, paramount, vital, prime, Stirring, eventful, august, sublime. For this is the way, I have read and heard, That authors look for the fitting word. All of the proud ingredients mine To build, like Marlowe, the mighty line. But never a line from my new-filled pen That couldn’t be done by a child of ten. Oh, how did Shelley and how did Keats Weave magic words on the fair white sheets Under conditions that, were they mine, I couldn’t bear? And I’d just resign. Yet Milton wrote passable literature Under conditions I couldn’t endure. Coleridge and Chatterton did their stuff Over a road that I’d christen rough. Wordsworth and—soft!—could it be that they Waited until they had something to say?

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Before, And, Roget

outputs.L1:
My desk is cleared of the litter of ages;  
Before me glitter the fair white pages.  
My fountain pen is clean and filled,  
And the noise of the office has long been stilled.  

Roget’s Thesaurus is close at hand,  
And I’m ready to do some work that’s grand—  
Dignified, eminent, great, momentous,  
Memorable, noteworthy, portentous,  
Beautiful, paramount, vital, prime,  
Stirring, eventful, august, sublime.  

For this is the way, I have read and heard,  
That authors search for the fitting word.  
All the proud ingredients are mine  
To build, like Marlowe, the mighty line.  

Yet never a line from my newly filled pen  
That couldn’t be written by a child of ten.  
Oh, how did Shelley, and how did Keats,  
Weave magic words on the fair white sheets  
Under conditions that, were they mine,  
I couldn’t bear? I would simply resign.  

Yet Milton wrote passable literature  
Under conditions I couldn’t endure.  
Coleridge and Chatterton did their stuff  
While traveling roads I would christen rough.  
Wordsworth and—soft!—could it be that they  
Waited until they had something to say?
outputs.L2:
My workspace has finally been purged of its ancient clutter. A stack of spotless paper gleams in front of me, my fountain pen has been washed and replenished with ink, and the office has been quiet for hours. With Roget’s Thesaurus close by, I am prepared to produce something magnificent—something noble, distinguished, important, unforgettable, remarkable, prophetic, lovely, supreme, essential, first-rate, exciting, historic, majestic, and exalted. After all, I have been told and have read that this is how writers discover precisely the right word.

I possess every impressive tool needed to forge a powerful verse worthy of Marlowe. Nevertheless, nothing produced by my freshly filled pen surpasses what a ten-year-old could write. How did Shelley and Keats cover blank pages with enchanted language while working in circumstances that would have driven me to quit? Milton, too, managed to create reasonably good literature in surroundings I would have found intolerable. Coleridge and Chatterton accomplished their work despite following a path I would certainly have called difficult. And Wordsworth and the others—wait, can it be? Perhaps they did not begin writing until they actually had an idea worth expressing.
outputs.L3:
The speaker carefully prepares what he considers the ideal environment for writing. He eliminates every possible distraction, lays out clean pages, makes sure his pen is filled, and keeps a thesaurus close at hand. With all these resources available, he hopes to produce grand, memorable literature, choosing impressive words that perfectly express his ideas.

Yet, despite the flawless conditions and careful preparation, the writing itself is disappointing. Instead of creating profound poetry or elegant prose, he manages only childish, uninspired lines. This failure leaves him puzzled, especially when he considers the famous poets of the past, many of whom produced great works while facing poverty, discomfort, illness, or other hardships. They wrote without the peaceful workspace and useful tools that he possesses.

In the end, the speaker recognizes that good writing does not come simply from perfect surroundings, abundant resources, or an impressive vocabulary. These things may support the creative process, but they cannot replace genuine thought or purpose. His realization is both simple and humbling: meaningful writing may depend above all on having something meaningful to say.
outputs.L4:
The would-be author approached writing as though it were a ceremony. Before setting down a single sentence, he arranged his desk beside the window, adjusted the lamp until its light fell at precisely the right angle, and placed a fresh notebook in the center of the polished wood. He made a pot of strong coffee, selected quiet instrumental music, and closed the door against every possible interruption. Surely, he thought, great work required perfect conditions.

Yet when he finally took up his pen, nothing came.

He stared at the blank page and imagined the great poets of the past composing immortal verses by candlelight or beneath ancient trees. Their words seemed effortless, dignified, and profound. His own first sentence looked painfully ordinary by comparison. He crossed it out and tried again, replacing simple words with elaborate ones. Whenever his language appeared too plain, he reached for the thesaurus and searched for something more impressive.

A “dark sky” became an “umbrageous firmament.” A man who “walked sadly” began to “perambulate in melancholy.” Soon every sentence was crowded with majestic adjectives and unfamiliar nouns. The author read the passage aloud, expecting to hear poetry. Instead, it sounded like a speech delivered by someone desperate to appear clever.

Dissatisfied, he changed his surroundings. Perhaps the chair was uncomfortable. Perhaps the coffee was too bitter. Perhaps the music was distracting. He opened the window, closed it again, sharpened three pencils, and rearranged the books on his desk. Then he returned to the page and compared his awkward phrases with lines written by the poets he admired.

The difference, he decided, was not merely talent. Their language carried feeling. Their words gave shape to grief, wonder, love, injustice, hope, and loss. They had not written beautifully because they possessed better desks or larger vocabularies. They had written beautifully because something within them demanded expression.

The would-be author looked again at his own page. Beneath all its decoration, it said nothing. He had been so concerned with sounding like a writer that he had forgotten to ask why he wished to write.

He put away the thesaurus. He turned off the music and let his coffee grow cold. Then he thought of a friend he had failed, a promise he regretted breaking, and the apology he had never found the courage to offer. At last, he began again.

This time the words were simple. They were also honest. One sentence led naturally to the next, and soon the blank page was no longer an enemy. The room had not become more comfortable, nor had he suddenly acquired the genius of the great poets. He had merely discovered something worth saying.

And that, he understood, was where powerful writing began.
outputs.L5:
**Before and After Roget**

Before Peter Mark Roget published his famous *Thesaurus* in 1852, writers searched for alternative words through memory, dictionaries, and scattered lists. Roget offered something new: he organized language by ideas rather than alphabet alone. Joy could lead to delight, pleasure, or elation; sorrow could become grief, anguish, or melancholy.

Roget’s work was more than a collection of synonyms. It became a bridge between thought **and** expression, helping people find the precise word for what they wished to say. Before Roget, the right word might remain hidden. After Roget, language seemed to open into a world of possibilities.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous poem about an aspiring author who prepares the perfect writing environment and consults Roget’s Thesaurus, only to realize that great poets succeeded because they actually had something to say.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Aspiring Bard**

He bought a desk of walnut grain,  
A chair designed to soothe the brain,  
A fountain pen, a leather book,  
A lamp with “literary” look.

He brewed a rare, exotic tea,  
Adjusted light to “poetry,”  
Lit sandalwood, then turned it down—  
Too mystical for verbs and nouns.

He placed Roget beside his chair  
To summon words both rich and rare:  
“Big” became “immense,” “colossal,”  
“Nice” turned “pleasing,” “fine,” “glossal.”

He sharpened pencils—twelve or twenty—  
Prepared for genius, ink aplenty.  
Then sat, composed, and stroked his chin,  
Awaiting Art to thunder in.

The clock ticked on. The tea went cold.  
No epic bloomed, no truth was told.  
He checked if Byron’s chair reclined,  
Or Keats required a snack to rhyme.

At last he read the poets, vexed,  
To learn what tools had made their text—  
And found, beneath each deathless phrase,  
No scented wax, no writer’s chaise.

They’d loved, rebelled, grieved, hoped, and bled;  
They had, in short, a thing to say.  
He sighed, shut dear Roget with care—  
Then wrote: **“I own a splendid chair.”**
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhyming satirical poem in which a writer sits before blank pages, lists grand synonyms, compares himself with Marlowe, Shelley, Keats, Milton, Coleridge, Chatterton, and Wordsworth, and ends with an ironic revelation.
counterfactuals.output:
Before a stack of pages, white and wide,  
A solemn scribbler dipped his pen in pride.  
“First, words!” he cried. “Let majesty commence:  
Sublime, august, transcendent, opulence!  

“Empyreal, ineffable, profound,  
Resplendent, orotund, and laurel-crowned;  
Ethereal, incandescent, sacrosanct—”  
He paused. The page remained serenely blank.  

“Marlowe had thunder; I have thunder too—  
Though his found verse, while mine awaits its cue.  
Like Shelley, I shall storm the tyrant sky,  
As soon as one auspicious phrase comes by.  

“With Keats I sip immortal vintage deep;  
I merely need a rhyme that isn’t ‘sleep.’  
Like Milton, I can justify God’s ways—  
Provided God allows me thirty days.  

“Coleridge had visions, opium, seas, and dread;  
I’ve coffee, indigestion, and a bed.  
Young Chatterton met glory in his doom;  
I meet the landlord knocking at my room.  

“Like Wordsworth, I find wisdom in a flower—  
Though staring at this daisy takes an hour.  
Yes, all the Muses breathe within my brain!”  
He flourished, frowned, and dipped his pen again.  

At last he wrote, with monumental look,  
A line to shake the age and crown his book;  
Then read the deathless sentence, proud and bright:  
“Dear Sir—my ink has failed. I cannot write.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lighthearted literary verse about writer’s block, contrasting a comfortable modern office worker with famous English poets who wrote under difficult conditions.
counterfactuals.output:
I sit in climate-controlled bliss,  
With lumbar support and peppermint tea,  
A blinking cursor asks for wit—  
I answer, “Try again at three.”

Poor Milton, blind, composed by ear;  
Young Keats wrote on while racked with cough;  
And Shakespeare, dodging plague each year,  
Still somehow knocked his sonnets off.

Yet here am I, with snacks arranged,  
Two screens, soft socks, a swivel chair;  
The font’s been tried, the playlist changed—  
No stubborn muse will fill the air.

Perhaps I’ll pace, as poets do,  
And suffer nobly down the hall—  
But first, one tiny task or two:  
Adjust the desk. Recheck the wall.

O bards who wrote through grief and gloom,  
Forgive my modern, cushioned plight:  
My greatest hardship in this room  
Is Wi-Fi dropping—one bar—tonight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
